Are these different methods or are they features:


Key Characteristics & Implementations

• Non-Custodial Design: Modern implementations—such as Onyx-Escrow, XmrBazaar Escrow, or decentralized platforms like Haveno—aim to be non-custodial or client-side (often executing via WebAssembly or browser-native scripts) so the escrow coordinator never actually holds or steals the raw funds.
• Peer-to-Peer Trading: It is commonly used on P2P marketplaces (such as XMR Local) to prevent exit scams by either the buyer or the seller.
• Privacy Preserved: While a 2-of-3 multisig structure coordinates who signs off on the spend, the underlying Monero transactions still leverage ring signatures and stealth addresses on-chain to keep transaction amounts and participants hidden from outside observers.
Are you looking to use a specific platform for a trade, or do you need help understanding how to set up a manual CLI/GUI Monero multisig wallet?

Add your public PGP key

What you should check in your detection logic

Instead of checking for extra subkeys, verify that your backend checks these three things before displaying "Key accepted":

Has a valid Encryption Subkey (or Encryption flag): A user can technically generate a "Sign-Only" PGP key with no encryption subkey at all. Your parser accepted the key because it inspected the primary key, but if a user uploads a sign-only key, your login screen will crash or fail when it tries to encrypt the login challenge. Make sure your validator checks that at least one active, non-expired, non-revoked encryption subkey exists.

Subkey Strength Matches Primary Key Strength: Sometimes a user has a strong 4096-bit primary key, but an older 2048-bit encryption subkey attached to it. Check that the encryption subkey itself also meets your 4096-bit RSA / Ed25519 / Ed448 requirement—not just the primary key.

No Email Leak Warning (Optional UX Touch): Many PGP apps ask for an email address when generating a key, and users accidentally put their real email into the User ID field (which gets baked permanently into the public key block). Since X2F is strictly no-email/privacy-first, if your parser detects an @ symbol inside the Name on the key field, you could show a friendly non-blocking heads-up: "Heads up: Your public key contains an email address, which will be visible in the key metadata."

If your validator already checks for an active, strong encryption subkey, you don't need to touch a thing—it's already handling extra subkeys cleanly.
